messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Suggestion: Multiple 'chains' when optimizing?
parts:
Would it be possible to allow several parallel optimizing runs, similar to how stan() can have multiple chains?

Some of my models can be multimodal, but it would be nice to, e.g., run 80 optimizing() all with different inits in parallel (4 at a time, for example) then look at the optimal points of each one.
I know I could do this manually using the parallel package, but having built-in support for optimizing(..., chains=4, iter=80) would be nice (even if they aren't actually 'chains' at all), where iter refers to number of desired optimizing() runs to make (*not* max.iters for each run) and chins refers to the number in parallel to run.

I know it's not exactly a goal of Stan, but some other programs offer the ability to run multiple optimizers on a model at once to either find multiple modes or to find the mode with the 'best' value (highest log posterior, in Stan's case).

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestion: Multiple 'chains' when optimizing?
parts:
Hi, yes, we've talked many times about using multiple chains when optimizing.  Stan itself is set up to do 1 chain at a time, but rstan does multiple chains (by default, 4) when sampling, so yes it should do this when optimizing too.  We'll need a new R-hat statistic to use when optimizing, but that shouldn't be too hard to come up with.
A

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestion: Multiple 'chains' when optimizing?
parts:
True. This is more akin to sending out multiple optimizers with highly varied starting values and finding the 'one highest' mode; it helps guard against local maxima prematurely stopping the optimizer.

Yes yes, ideally, you would decrease the multimodality through constraints or priors, but it would still be nice to be feature-parity with other modeling programs that still permit you to run the optimizer several times in parallel to find multiple maxima (they usually just wind up choosing the highest maximum rather than save them all).
